title: Is the Rice Yield Response to Elevated CO₂ a Source Effect or a Sink Effect?
content: Rice feeds more than half of humanity, yet whether its yield gain under elevated CO₂ comes from a stronger source or a larger sink is unresolved, because the two are seldom measured together. From 6,120 Web of Science (WoS) and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) records we built an evidence map; 668 met all criteria, revealing the publication was unbalanced: 460 studies (68.9%) measured source traits against 194 (29.0%) for sink traits (2.37:1); harvest index (HI) appeared in only 22 (3.3%). The split repeats in both language subsets: it reflects the field, not the databases. Seven syntheses gave photosynthesis +21.9%, panicle biomass +25.4%, little change in grain mass or HI, and grain yield +12-20% under free-air CO₂ enrichment (FACE). Extra biomass went to roots (+8.5%) and away from leaves (-8.4%). Partly disjoint and non-independent, the estimates are listed side by side, not combined. The pattern fits sequential constraints: CO₂ enlarges sink number before heading; grain filling responds little. By quantifying this source bias and locating the thinnest evidence, the map re-directs experiment, breeding and modelling to the sink, where the yield still to be won lies.
